title: Anemia: What It Is and Why It Happens
content:
Anemia is a condition where the body doesn't have enough healthy red blood cells, or those cells don't carry enough hemoglobin, the iron-rich protein that binds oxygen and gives blood its red color. Because red blood cells are the body's main way of delivering oxygen to tissues, anemia effectively reduces how efficiently oxygen reaches muscles, organs, and the brain — which explains most of its symptoms.

Anemia has three broad categories of cause: the body losing blood faster than it can replace it, the body not producing enough red blood cells in the first place, or red blood cells being destroyed faster than normal. Within those categories, specific causes vary widely. Blood loss can be obvious (an injury, surgery, or heavy menstrual bleeding) or subtle and easy to miss over time (slow gastrointestinal bleeding, for example). Reduced production can result from nutritional deficiencies (most commonly iron, but also vitamin B12 or folate), chronic diseases that suppress red blood cell production, bone marrow disorders, or certain medications. Increased destruction of red blood cells happens in some inherited conditions and some autoimmune or infectious processes.

By far the most common cause worldwide is a lack of sufficient iron, since the body needs iron as a building block for hemoglobin. This is often called iron-deficiency anemia and is covered in more detail in a related article, but it's worth noting here because it's the type most people will encounter.

Symptoms of anemia depend heavily on how severe it is and how quickly it developed. Mild anemia, or anemia that develops gradually, often causes few or no noticeable symptoms — the body adapts. As it becomes more pronounced, common symptoms include fatigue and low energy, feeling unusually cold, dizziness or lightheadedness (especially when standing up quickly), irritability, shortness of breath with activity that wouldn't normally cause it, headache, and pale skin or pale inner eyelids. Because these symptoms overlap heavily with many other conditions — thyroid problems, poor sleep, and general stress can all cause similar fatigue — anemia is usually confirmed with blood testing rather than symptoms alone.

The standard first test is a complete blood count (CBC), which reports hemoglobin concentration along with other red blood cell measurements. If hemoglobin comes back below the typical reference range for a person's age and sex, further testing often follows to identify the underlying cause — for example, iron studies (including ferritin, a marker of the body's iron stores) if iron deficiency is suspected, or vitamin B12 and folate levels if those are more likely given the clinical picture.

Treatment depends entirely on the cause: iron-deficiency anemia is typically treated with iron supplementation and addressing the source of iron loss (such as heavy periods); vitamin-deficiency anemias are treated with the relevant supplement; anemia from chronic disease often improves as the underlying condition is managed. Because the right treatment depends on correctly identifying why the anemia is happening, self-treating with iron supplements before that's established isn't recommended — in some cases it can mask or delay finding the real cause. This is general information, not a diagnosis; a low hemoglobin result on a lab report is a starting point for a conversation with a clinician, not a conclusion on its own.
